# General principles of fractures

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > General orthopedics > General principles of fractures*

[Original Article Link](/library/T3063f)

---

## Summary

A fracture is a partial or complete interruption in the continuity of bone. The most common cause is trauma, followed by diseases that result in weakened bone structure. Fractures are named and classified according to a variety of characteristics, including location, extent, and orientation. Evaluation of a suspected fracture includes obtaining a <u>patient history</u> and assessing the <u>skin</u>, <u>soft tissue</u>, and sensory and <u>motor function</u> of the affected area. Fractures are typically diagnosed on <u>x-ray</u>; <u>CT scan</u> and <u>MRI</u> are helpful adjuncts for surgical planning and diagnosis of subtle or <u>occult fractures</u>. Acute management consists of <u>analgesia</u>, <u>wound care</u>, <u>fracture reduction</u>, and <u>immobilization</u>. <u>Surgery</u> may be necessary. <u>Open fractures</u>, in which the bone is exposed due to severe <u>soft tissue</u> injury, require urgent surgical management and <u>antibiotic therapy</u>. Acute complications include nerve and vascular injury, hemorrhage, and <u>acute compartment syndrome</u> (<u>ACS</u>); long-term complications include <u>avascular necrosis</u> and <u>nonunion</u>.




The specific management of different fracture types is covered in separate articles; see “<u>Overview of common fractures</u>” for links. See also “<u>Management of trauma patients</u>” and “<u>Conservative management of fractures</u>.”

---

## Etiology

* Trauma: mechanical <u>stress</u> and/or loading

* Weakened bone structure: <u>osteoporosis</u>, bone tumors, <u>metastasis</u>, Paget disease





References:[[1]](/library/IM0YJg)

---

## Classification

Fractures are typically classified based on the following characteristics: [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)




* Anatomy

* Location: affected bone (<u>proximal</u>, <u>distal</u>)

* Position: <u>diaphysis</u>, <u>metaphysis</u>, <u>epiphysis</u>

* Extent  

* Complete

* Incomplete

* Orientation: transverse, oblique, spiral

* Displacement 

* Rotated: rotation around the <u>longitudinal axis</u>

* Angulated: angulation of the axis

* Translated: <u>lateral</u> movement of the bone fragments

* Longitudinal displacement of bone fragments

* Distraction: elongation

* Impaction: shortening

* Fragmentation

* Comminuted fracture: more than two fracture lines resulting in multiple bone fragments

* Segmental fracture: two fracture lines with a bone fragment between the <u>proximal</u> and <u>distal</u> portions of the bone

* <u>Soft tissue</u> involvement

* Closed fracture (simple fracture; does not come into contact with the outside environment)

* <u>Open fracture</u>

* Stability [[3]](/library/OaWIkP0)

* Stable fractures

* Bone fragments remain in their normal anatomical alignment without significant displacement from their original position.

* Low risk of progression to <u>dislocation</u> or conversion to <u>open fractures</u>

* Unstable fractures

* Bone fragments are significantly displaced, misaligned, or shifted from normal <u>anatomical position</u>.

* High risk of displacement after reduction and of complications or compromised healing

* <u>Growth plate</u> involvement (<u>pediatric fractures</u>): <u>Salter-Harris fractures</u>





> [!TIP]
> To describe the features of a fracture, think NOLARD: Neurovascular status, Open vs. closed, Location, Angulation-Alignment-Articular, Rotation, Displacement. [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)

## Overview of common fractures

For <u>common fractures in children</u> (e.g., <u>greenstick fractures</u>), see “<u>Pediatric fractures</u>.”




### Upper extremity fractures




* <u>Humerus fractures</u>

* <u>Elbow fractures</u>

* <u>Forearm fractures</u>

* <u>Monteggia fracture</u>

* <u>Galeazzi fracture</u>

* Wrist fractures (<u>distal radius fractures</u>)

* <u>Colles fracture</u>

* <u>Smith fracture</u>

* Hand fractures

* <u>Metacarpal fractures</u> (e.g., boxer's fracture)

* <u>Scaphoid fracture</u>

* <u>Phalangeal fractures</u>





### Lower extremity fractures




* <u>Hip fractures</u>

* <u>Femoral head fracture</u>

* <u>Femoral neck fracture</u>

* <u>Femoral shaft fracture</u>

* <u>Tibial fracture</u>

* <u>Ankle fracture</u>

* Foot fractures

* Midfoot fracture (<u>Lisfranc fracture</u>): a tarsometatarsal fracture; may involve damage to the <u>cartilage</u> of the midfoot <u>joints</u>

* Jones fracture: fracture at the base of the shaft of the fifth <u>metatarsal</u> bone

* <u>Talus fracture</u>

* <u>Calcaneal fracture</u>





### Truncal fractures




* <u>Clavicle fracture</u>

* <u>Sternal fracture</u>

* <u>Rib fracture</u>

* <u>Vertebral fractures</u> (including compression fracture)

* <u>Pelvic fracture</u>





### Head and neck fractures




* <u>Skull fractures</u>

* <u>Basilar skull fracture</u>

* <u>Temporal bone fracture</u>

* <u>Facial fractures</u>

* <u>Le Fort fractures</u>

* <u>Nasal bone fracture</u>

* <u>Mandibular fracture</u>

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Pain</u> localized to the fracture site

* Redness and swelling

* Limb deformity

* Palpable step-off or gap

* Bone <u>crepitus</u>

* <u>Ecchymosis</u>

* Possible neurovascular compromise below the site of injury

* Possible <u>signs of an open fracture</u>

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[4]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Conduct a thorough history  and <u>physical examination</u>.

* Perform a <u>neurovascular assessment</u> to check for <u>neurovascular injury</u> and <u>compartment syndrome</u>.

* Obtain <u>x-rays</u> of the affected extremity in at least two orthogonal views.

* Consider advanced imaging (CT or <u>MRI</u>) in consultation with orthopedics (e.g., for suspected <u>occult fractures</u>).

* Obtain <u>preoperative diagnostics</u> if fractures are likely to require urgent operative treatment.





> [!WARNING]
> Any findings that suggest <u>neurovascular injury</u> or <u>open fracture</u> should prompt urgent orthopedic consultation.




> [!TIP]
> Fractures associated with gross deformities and/or <u>crepitus</u> should be splinted prior to imaging. [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)




### Neurovascular assessment [[5]](/library/C1WqQ40)[[6]](/library/ogW0wk0)




* Purpose: detecting early signs of limb <u>ischemia</u>, <u>peripheral nerve injury</u>, or <u>compartment syndrome</u>

* Components

* Sensation

* <u>Motor function</u>

* <u>Perfusion</u>

* Findings

* See “<u>Nerve injuries in the upper body</u>.”

* See “<u>Nerve injuries in the lower body</u>.”

* Acute <u>ischemia</u>/<u>ACS</u>: <u>6 Ps of ALI</u>





> [!TIP]
> A <u>neurovascular assessment</u> should be performed in all patients with extremity injuries and repeated after every intervention (e.g., reduction or <u>immobilization</u>). [[5]](/library/C1WqQ40)

### Imaging [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[7]](/library/2A1TQj0)




#### <u>X-ray</u>




* Indication: all suspected fractures (before and after reduction)

* Views

* All extremities: at least two orthogonal views (e.g., AP and <u>lateral</u>)

* Some sites may benefit from a dedicated third view (e.g., oblique view, notch view of the knee)

* Consider imaging of <u>joints</u> above and below a suspected fracture.

* Radiographic fracture signs

* Disruption of bony cortex

* <u>Radiolucent</u> fracture line

* Fracture fragments in <u>comminuted fractures</u>

* Specific fracture findings, e.g. <u>elbow fat pad signs</u> , height loss in <u>vertebral fractures</u>





> [!WARNING]
> As fractures may not be visible on <u>x-rays</u> for up to two weeks after an injury, any focal bony tenderness after a severe injury should initially be treated as a fracture. [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)

#### Additional imaging modalities [[4]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Point-of-care ultrasound</u> (<u>POCUS</u>): potential alternative to <u>x-ray</u> in patients who wish to avoid radiation or when <u>x-ray</u> is unavailable   [[8]](/library/JgWswk0)

* CT 

* Inconclusive <u>x-ray</u> findings: may be indicated

* Assessment of associated injuries

* Preoperative planning for complicated fractures

* <u>MRI</u>: may be indicated to diagnose associated <u>tendon</u>/<u>ligament injuries</u> or <u>occult fracture</u>

## Treatment

### Initial fracture management [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[4]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Immobilization</u>

* Immobilize <u>joints</u> above and below for most extremity fractures.

* <u>Splint</u> in the position of function (if not otherwise specified).

* See “<u>Conservative treatment of fractures</u>” for details.

* Indications to consult orthopedics for fractures  [[7]](/library/2A1TQj0)

* Any signs of neurovascular compromise or <u>compartment syndrome</u>

* <u>Open fractures</u>

* Displaced intraarticular fractures

* <u>Fracture-dislocations</u>

* Associated <u>tendon</u> injury

* <u>Supportive care</u>

* Provide adequate <u>analgesia</u>.

* Perform <u>wound care</u> (see “<u>Acute wound management</u>”).

* Initiate <u>antibiotic prophylaxis for open fractures</u>.

* Admit or discharge with proper follow-up (see “Disposition” below).





> [!WARNING]
> Fractures with <u>skin tenting</u> should be reduced promptly to prevent conversion to an <u>open fracture</u>. [[7]](/library/2A1TQj0)




### Analgesia for acute fractures [[7]](/library/2A1TQj0)[[9]](/library/Z71Z4R0)




* Nonoperative and/or outpatient management

* <u>Non-opioid analgesics</u>

* <u>Acetaminophen</u> DOSAGE [[9]](/library/Z71Z4R0)

* <u>NSAIDs</u>: e.g., <u>ibuprofen</u> DOSAGE  [[9]](/library/Z71Z4R0)

* <u>Gabapentin</u> DOSAGE [[9]](/library/Z71Z4R0)

* <u>Opioid analgesics</u>: typically reserved for <u>long bone</u> fractures and/or severe <u>pain</u> 

* <u>Tramadol</u> DOSAGE [[9]](/library/Z71Z4R0)

* <u>Hydrocodone</u>/<u>acetaminophen</u> DOSAGE [[9]](/library/Z71Z4R0)

* For prescribing principles and risk mitigation strategies, see “<u>Opioids for acute pain</u>.”

* Operative and/or inpatient management

* <u>NSAIDs</u>, e.g. <u>ketorolac</u> IV DOSAGE followed by <u>ibuprofen</u> PO DOSAGE [[9]](/library/Z71Z4R0)

* <u>Combination analgesics</u>, e.g. <u>oxycodone</u>/<u>acetaminophen</u> DOSAGE [[9]](/library/Z71Z4R0)

* <u>Opioids</u> for severe <u>pain</u>, e.g. <u>hydromorphone</u> DOSAGE [[9]](/library/Z71Z4R0)

* Additional interventions

* <u>Cryotherapy</u>: Ice pack for 20–30 minutes every 1–2 hours.  [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)

* Consider <u>procedural sedation</u> and/or <u>regional anesthesia</u> before interventions.

* Ensure proper <u>immobilization</u> of the fracture to reduce <u>pain</u> associated with movement.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Analgesics</u> are typically only needed for 2–5 days following an injury. Consider a fracture complication if significant <u>pain</u> persists beyond this time frame. [[7]](/library/2A1TQj0)




### Nonoperative fracture management [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)




* Indications

* <u>Stable fractures</u> without neurovascular compromise

* Most <u>pediatric fractures</u>

* Procedure

* <u>Closed reduction</u>

* Long-term <u>immobilization</u> with a cast or <u>splint</u>

* See “<u>Conservative treatment of fractures</u>” for <u>supportive care</u> and additional considerations.





### Surgical fracture management




* Indications [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)

* <u>Open fractures</u>

* Associated arterial injury

* Severe displacement (e.g., rotational deformities) with displaced fragments

* Inadequate manual reduction and fixation

* <u>Unstable fractures</u>

* Displaced intraarticular fractures

* Fracture within <u>metastatic</u> lesion

* Procedure: anatomical reduction of the fracture and subsequent fixation and <u>immobilization</u>  

* <u>External fixation</u>

* <u>Immobilization</u> of a fracture using pins or screws that are secured outside of the <u>skin</u>

* Commonly performed as a temporary measure in severely injured patients or contaminated <u>open fractures</u>

* <u>Internal fixation</u>

* <u>Immobilization</u> of a fracture using implants (e.g., plates, screws, wires)

* Can be performed in combination with closed or <u>open reduction</u>

* See “<u>Osteosynthetic procedures</u>” for details.





### Disposition [[4]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Discharge considerations

* Consider discharge with <u>supportive care</u> for:

* Stable nonoperative fractures

* <u>Stable fractures</u> after successful <u>closed reduction</u>

* Arrange follow-up with orthopedics in 3–5 days.

* Indications for admission 

* Urgent operative management needed

* Severe intractable <u>pain</u>

* Inability to safely ambulate or perform <u>activities of daily living</u>

* Specialist referral

* Orthopedics: <u>casting</u>, reassessment, and operative planning

* <u>Podiatry</u>: management of foot fractures

* Physical medicine and <u>rehabilitation</u>: postfracture <u>rehabilitation</u>

---

## Complications

### Acute complications [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[7]](/library/2A1TQj0)




* <u>Acute compartment syndrome</u>

* <u>Neurovascular injury</u> (e.g., nerve injury, bleeding, <u>hematoma</u>, <u>seroma</u>)

* Fracture blisters 

* Clear or hemorrhagic <u>blister</u> that can develop between 6 hours and 3 weeks after injury; most commonly after 24–48 hours

* May delay intervention because of increased risk of infection and <u>wound dehiscence</u> and should be left intact

* Wound infection

* <u>Osteomyelitis</u>

* Secondary <u>dislocation</u>

* <u>Fat embolism</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Closed <u>femur</u> fractures and <u>pelvic fractures</u> may be associated with significant hemorrhage requiring <u>transfusion</u>. [[7]](/library/2A1TQj0)




> [!WARNING]
> Suspect <u>compartment syndrome</u> in patients with intense or <u>disproportionate pain</u> (e.g., <u>pain</u> with passive stretch), even in the absence of additional symptoms. [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)




![Compartment syndrome of the lower leg](media/g3oq9cvdmc6rogpboka2uc16.jpg)

Compartment syndrome of the lower leg

![Fracture blisters](media/oilgq6xxixck8gqv09c6cdy0.jpg)

Fracture blisters

![Postoperative infection of the ankle](media/n91g8jnfid0upt3swyo53j6j.jpg)

Postoperative infection of the ankle




### <u>Complications due to immobilization</u> [[10]](/library/BgWzxk0)[[11]](/library/oK10h30)




* <u>Thrombosis</u> (e.g., <u>DVT</u>, <u>pulmonary embolism</u>)

* Muscle <u>atrophy</u>

* <u>Joint contractures</u>

* Cardiovascular <u>deconditioning</u>

* <u>Decubitus ulcer</u>

* Infections, e.g.:

* <u>Pneumonia</u>

* <u>Urinary tract infection</u>





### Complications of nonweightbearing




* Muscle <u>atrophy</u>

* <u>Crutch palsy</u>





### Compromised <u>fracture healing</u>




#### Nonunion [[12]](/library/tgWXCk0)




* Definition: incomplete healing of a fracture; can result in the creation of a false <u>joint</u> (<u>pseudarthrosis</u>)

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Poor vascular supply

* Inadequate <u>immobilization</u>

* Chronic diseases (e.g., <u>diabetes mellitus</u>, <u>osteoporosis</u>)

* <u>Open fractures</u>

* Infection

* Smoking

* Types [[13]](/library/YSWnyk0)

* <u>Hypertrophic</u> <u>nonunion</u>: <u>callus</u> formation in the fracture zone

* <u>Atrophic</u> <u>nonunion</u>: <u>atrophic</u> bone without <u>callus</u> formation

* Clinical features

* <u>Pain</u> and swelling

* Limited <u>weight-bearing</u> capacity

* Reduced <u>range of motion</u> that persists

* Diagnosis: Imaging shows lack of fracture consolidation 6–9 months after injury.

* Treatment [[14]](/library/GgWB9k0)

* <u>Debridement</u> and resection

* Osteosynthesis (fixation)

* Culture-directed <u>antibiotics</u> for infected <u>nonunion</u>





![Hypertrophic pseudarthrosis of the distal fibula](media/rjk6n906qrn6p0t9gglfgr92.jpg)

Hypertrophic pseudarthrosis of the distal fibula

![Left femoral neck pseudathrosis](media/am6fefdue9ufegkb791jnkep.jpg)

Left femoral neck pseudathrosis

![Hypertrophic nonunion of humeral fracture (1/2)](media/wow8pouyy85crm0bsk7w1l2t.jpg)

Hypertrophic nonunion of humeral fracture (1/2)

![Hypertrophic nonunion of humeral fracture (2/2)](media/w5m47dk6l8elh7e7sudz2f0i.jpg)

Hypertrophic nonunion of humeral fracture (2/2)




#### Malunion [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[15]](/library/NaW-kP0)




* Definition: healing of a fracture in a pathological position

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Inadequate <u>immobilization</u>

* Inaccurate reduction

* Unsuccessful surgical fixation

* Clinical features

* <u>Pain</u> and swelling

* Impairment of function

* Limb shortening (poorly tolerated in the lower extremities)

* Treatment: surgical correction (<u>osteotomy</u>) in symptomatic patients





### Long-term complications




* Growth disturbances after <u>growth plate fracture</u> in children

* <u>Chronic osteomyelitis</u>

* <u>Avascular necrosis</u>

* Posttraumatic <u>osteoarthritis</u>

* <u>Complex regional pain syndrome</u>

* <u>Joint</u> stiffness/<u>contracture</u>

* <u>Joint</u> instability

* <u>Heterotopic ossification</u>





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Subtypes and variants

Specific types of fractures that require modified approaches to diagnostics and treatment include <u>open fractures</u> and <u>pathologic fractures</u>.




### Open fracture [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[7]](/library/2A1TQj0)




#### Definition




* A fracture with direct communication to the outside environment via a break in the <u>skin</u> and <u>soft tissue</u>

* Typically caused by high-energy trauma





#### Clinical features of open fractures




* <u>Soft tissue</u> injuries: <u>open wound</u> or puncture

* Visible bone fragments in an <u>open wound</u>

* Visibly greasy, fatty, or oily blood loss





![Open fracture of the right ankle](media/v5nxge489fgssfi8n2tpjiug.jpg)

Open fracture of the right ankle

![Open fracture of the left ankle](media/kw6c1ulxmf7cuc8ltqtvtkad.jpg)

Open fracture of the left ankle




#### Diagnostics




* Clinical evaluation

* Examine fractures closely for signs of <u>skin</u> and <u>soft tissue</u> compromise.

* Perform a thorough <u>neurovascular examination</u>.

* Imaging

* <u>X-ray</u> of the fracture and surrounding <u>joints</u>: Air may be detected in the <u>soft tissue</u>. [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)

* Consider CT (e.g., for periarticular injuries).





#### Treatment [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[4]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Acute wound management</u> and <u>immobilization</u>

* Remove visible foreign bodies and debris.

* Irrigate wound with sterile saline if operative <u>irrigation</u> will be performed > 2 hours postinjury.

* Cover with moist, <u>sterile dressing</u> and <u>splint</u> the fractured extremity.

* Perform <u>tetanus prophylaxis</u> if <u>vaccine</u> status is outdated or unknown.

* Emergent orthopedic referral

* Operative <u>irrigation</u> and <u>debridement</u> within 24 hours of injury

* <u>Tuft fractures</u> with small, clean wounds may be managed in the ED with <u>irrigation</u> and <u>debridement</u>.

* Antibiotic prophylaxis for open fractures: Initiate as soon as possible after injury. [[16]](/library/9gWNxk0)[[17]](/library/oaW0lP0)

* Most injuries without gross contamination: Gram-positive coverage suffices.

* <u>First-generation cephalosporins</u>, e.g., <u>cefazolin</u> DOSAGE [[17]](/library/oaW0lP0)

* For patients with <u>penicillin</u> <u>allergy</u>: e.g., <u>clindamycin</u> DOSAGE [[17]](/library/oaW0lP0)

* Severe/extensive injuries: Consider broader coverage, e.g., with <u>ceftriaxone</u>. DOSAGE  [[16]](/library/9gWNxk0)[[17]](/library/oaW0lP0)[[18]](/library/2SWT_k0)

* Duration: 24 hours unless active infection develops [[16]](/library/9gWNxk0)





> [!WARNING]
> Fractures associated with wounds directly over the site, even if minor, should be treated as <u>open fractures</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Operative management of <u>open fractures</u> should be performed promptly because of the high risk of <u>osteomyelitis</u>.




### Pathologic fracture [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)




#### Definition



* A fracture due to abnormal bone <u>weakness</u> caused by an underlying condition; may be spontaneous or secondary to minor trauma   [[19]](/library/bSWHyk0)




#### Etiology




* Disorders affecting bone metabolism, e.g., <u>osteoporosis</u> (most common cause), <u>hyperparathyroidism</u>

* Bone lesions

* <u>Malignant bone tumors</u> and <u>bone metastases</u>  [[20]](/library/wgWhxk0)

* <u>Benign bone tumors</u> (including bone cysts)

* Malignant blood diseases (e.g., <u>multiple myeloma</u>)

* Infection: <u>chronic osteomyelitis</u>





#### Common locations [[19]](/library/bSWHyk0)




* <u>Proximal</u> <u>femur</u>

* <u>Proximal</u> <u>humerus</u>

* <u>Spine</u> (<u>vertebral compression fractures</u>)





#### Clinical features




* <u>Pain</u> localized over fracture site

* Occasionally painless swelling over fracture site

* Systemic symptoms (e.g., fatigue, unexplained weight loss)

* Generalized bone <u>pain</u>





#### Diagnostics




* <u>X-ray</u> findings (depending on the underlying cause)

* Bone lesions

* Thinning of the cortices

* Generalized <u>osteopenia</u>

* Other imaging modalities: CT, <u>MRI</u>





![Pathologic fracture](media/bmqgx8eekk23pcniuvh6u0ux.jpg)

Pathologic fracture

![Pathologic femoral fracture](media/kkdpy2qvtjrgsimszm5jbxix.jpg)

Pathologic femoral fracture




#### Treatment




* Initial treatment aligns with <u>general fracture care</u>.

* Further management depends on location and etiology.





### Other




* Avulsion fracture  [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[21]](/library/MaWMOP0)

* A fracture caused by bone shearing at the insertion point of a <u>tendon</u> or <u>ligament</u>

* Most commonly due to ligamentous <u>traction</u>; can be acute  or chronic

* May be associated with <u>joint</u> instability due to <u>ligament injury</u>

* Surgical management may be necessary for significantly displaced fracture fragments or injury to other structures.

* Periprosthetic fracture  [[22]](/library/wSWhbO0)

* A fracture directly adjacent to an orthopedic implant; most commonly due to low-energy trauma

* <u>Stable fractures</u> with fixed hardware are managed with <u>immobilization</u> and restricted <u>weight-bearing</u>.

* <u>Unstable fractures</u> and/or loose prostheses require surgical revision.

* Occult fracture

* A fracture that is not radiographically evident following an injury

* Common locations include the <u>scaphoid</u> and hip.

* If an <u>occult fracture</u> is suspected, <u>general fracture care</u> (including <u>immobilization</u>) should be initiated.

* <u>Stress fracture</u>

* Fracture of structurally normal bone due to repetitive microtrauma

* See “<u>Stress fractures</u>” for details.

* <u>Greenstick fracture</u>

* Type of <u>incomplete fracture</u>; common in children

* See “<u>Pediatric fractures</u>” for details.

* Fractures suggesting abuse: See “<u>Injuries suggestive of child abuse</u>” for patterns that may indicate <u>physical child abuse</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Accessory ossicles</u> are sometimes mistaken for <u>avulsion fractures</u>, but they can be differentiated by their smooth borders. [[2]](/library/zr1rPR0)
